title: NP-hardness of Euclidean covering radius
formal: Is exact Euclidean lattice covering radius NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time map sending each Boolean 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a rational full-column-rank matrix \(B\) and a positive rational threshold \(r\), such that \[\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu_2(L(B))\le r?\] Unsatisfiable formulas must map to instances with \(\mu_2(L(B))>r\). This is the exact decision problem, with approximation factor one and no promised gap between the two cases.

source_formulation.text: In particular, we reiterate that the problem of showing NP-hardness of exact GapCRP in the l2 norm (the most important special case) remains open.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 7

why: The covering radius measures how far a point can be from its nearest lattice point. It is a central lattice invariant with connections to integer programming and to worst-case lattice problems used in cryptography. Establishing even exact Euclidean NP-hardness would close a basic gap in the complexity classification of lattice problems, without requiring the stronger approximation-hardness results known in other norms.
status_note: The proceedings paper published on 9 September 2026 explicitly lists exact Euclidean covering-radius NP-hardness as open. Its new large-norm hardness theorem does not cover p=2. The bounded search through 2026-09-15 found no verified resolution of this exact deterministic many-one decision target; it is not exhaustive certification of current openness.

progress.text: As reviewed in the 2026 paper, Haviv and Regev obtain stronger hierarchy hardness for the infinity norm and sufficiently large finite norms; a 2012 journal version follows.
Bennett and Ly publish explicit finite-\(p\) hardness thresholds while retaining exact Euclidean NP-hardness as an open question in Section 1.4.

category_assignment.reason: The restored task is exact Euclidean lattice covering radius hardness.

importance.reason: Exact covering radius is a basic geometric invariant of lattices, yet even NP-hardness in the Euclidean norm is unresolved in the 2026 source. A classification would settle a central lattice-complexity question and clarify the contrast with large-norm hardness; the question also sits within the geometry underlying lattice cryptography and integer programming.

sentences: A lattice covering radius is the largest distance from a point in its span to the nearest lattice point.
The input here is a rational basis and a positive rational threshold in the Euclidean norm.
The exact decision problem accepts precisely when the covering radius is at most the threshold.
The question asks whether satisfiability reduces to this decision problem by one deterministic polynomial-time map.
A September 2026 paper proves hardness for sufficiently large norms while explicitly leaving the Euclidean case open.

definitions: The input basis is a matrix \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), where \(m\ge n\ge1\) and the \(n\) columns are linearly independent over \(\mathbb R\). Its lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\). For \(v\in\mathbb R^m\), the Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^m v_j^2)^{1/2}\). Define \[\mu_2(L(B))=\sup_{t\in\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(B)}\inf_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\|t-Bz\|_2=\max_{w\in[0,1]^n}\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\|B(w-z)\|_2.\] The points \(t\) range over the real linear span of the lattice, not the whole ambient space when \(n<m\). The compact fundamental parallelepiped \(B[0,1]^n\) gives the equivalent finite-radius maximum. The minimum ranges over all integer combinations, including coefficients outside \(\{0,1\}\). The exact decision language contains precisely valid pairs \((B,r)\) with \(r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\) and \(\mu_2(L(B))\le r\); equality is a YES instance and any strict excess is a NO instance. Encode dimensions and signed rational numerators and positive denominators in binary, with explicit delimiters and all matrix entries listed. Complexity is measured in total encoding length, including entry precision and the threshold, not just dimension. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three Boolean variables or their negations, with variable indices encoded in binary; it is satisfiable when some Boolean assignment makes every clause true. The requested reduction is one finite deterministic Turing-machine program with a fixed polynomial bit-time bound. It must output a valid instance on every valid formula, and the equivalence must hold for all formulas. All output bits and exact rational arithmetic costs count. No oracle, advice, randomness, real-number oracle or unbounded-precision unit-cost arithmetic is available. NP-hardness here is deterministic many-one hardness for every language with a polynomial-time verifier and polynomial-length witnesses, equivalently hardness for the specified 3-SAT language.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a reduction exists, including polynomial bit complexity, valid output bases and both directions of the satisfiability equivalence, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation. A proof of a polynomial-time algorithm would refute NP-hardness only with an appropriate complexity separation; it is not by itself a negative answer. Hardness in another norm, hardness of linear discrepancy or of coding-theoretic covering radius, randomized reductions alone, and a reduction that reverses YES and NO do not establish this target. The task does not require NP membership or a quantitative approximation gap.

context_blocks.text: Bennett and Ly explicitly single out NP-hardness of exact \(\ell_2\) covering radius in Section 1.4 of their September 2026 proceedings paper. Definition 4 specifies the decision orientation: small covering radius is YES, while radius strictly above the threshold is NO.

Their new hardness theorem applies for fixed \(p>p_0\), where \(p_0\approx35.31\), in the norm \(\|v\|_p=(\sum_j|v_j|^p)^{1/p}\). It gives approximation hardness with factors greater than one for suitable parameters. The Euclidean value \(p=2\) lies outside that theorem.

The paper distinguishes covering radius from linear discrepancy, \(\max_{w\in[0,1]^n}\min_{z\in\{0,1\}^n}\|B(w-z)\|_p\). Restricting the nearest point to binary combinations can change the value, even when the generated lattice is unchanged. The present question uses all lattice points.

The introduction relates approximate covering radius to worst-case lattice problems and integer programming. These connections motivate the complexity question but do not supply a hardness proof for the exact Euclidean decision language.
